title: Optimally embedded tight binding for reproducing geometry dependent observables
authors: Jonas J Telle, Gunnar F Lange
abstract: In tight-binding models, the position operator is reduced to intra-cell orbital positions (embeddings). While accurately reproducing band structures, such models often fail for geometry dependent responses depending on the position operator. To address this, we investigate the role of these embeddings and introduce the general framework of optimally embedded tight binding. Treating the embeddings as geometric tuning parameters to be fixed against a reference response (obtained from ab-initio computation or experiment), we obtain tight-binding models of GaAs and CdS which quantitatively reproduce non-linear optical responses at no cost to band structure accuracy. The optimal embeddings are determined efficiently using position derivatives obtained from decomposing tight-binding observables into a geometry independent and dependent part, and explicit derivatives are provided for key quantities such as the quantum geometric tensor. The decomposition reveals where geometric effects dominate, and we show in both toy models and in the Chern insulator V2O3 how geometry can dramatically alter the local metric trace. Our results highlight that orbital embeddings should be treated as a genuine model parameter which should be explicitly fixed against physical data to get accurate minimal models.
summary: This paper addresses the limitation of tight-binding models that fail when calculating properties sensitive to spatial geometry, despite accurately predicting band structures. The authors propose an 'optimally embedded' framework, treating orbital positions as tunable parameters fixed against experimental or ab-initio data. This allows for the construction of highly accurate minimal models capable of reproducing complex geometric observables like optical responses.
main_problem: Tight-binding models fail to accurately reproduce geometry-dependent physical responses, even when they correctly model geometry-independent properties like band structures.
main_result: The authors introduce an 'optimally embedded tight binding' framework where orbital embeddings are treated as explicit tuning parameters fixed against reference data to achieve accurate minimal models.
method: They determine optimal embeddings by decomposing observable quantities into geometry-independent and dependent parts, utilizing position derivatives for efficient fitting.
model_or_system: The study uses solid-state systems modeled via tight-binding theory (e.g., GaAs, CdS), focusing on the Hamiltonian structure derived from Bloch states and incorporating orbital embeddings ($	au_\alpha$).
key_observables: Non-linear optical responses ($\sigma(\omega)$), quantum geometric tensor, and local metric trace.
important_parameters: Orbital embedding parameters ($\{	au_\alpha\}$) are the key tunable parameters.
main_assumptions: The initial approximation assumes orbitals are nearly point-like; the method requires fixing embeddings against external physical data (ab-initio or experiment).
figures_summary: Figures compare optical responses using different embedding models and show that fitting optimal embeddings on a coarse grid successfully reproduces the true, dense response.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the failure of standard tight-binding models for geometry dependence. It then introduces the optimal embedding framework, detailing the mathematical decomposition used to tune parameters against physical observables, culminating in successful quantitative reproduction of optical responses.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state physics, the methodology—treating geometric structure (embeddings) as tunable model parameters fixed by external data to improve predictive power—is a general concept applicable to parameterizing complex quantum systems where full first-principles calculation is prohibitive.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of main results. (a) A tight-binding model can be viewed as a weighted graph, where hoppings and on-site terms are represented by edges and loops. (b) Specifying the orbital positions τα amounts to embedding this graph in real space. (c)–(e) Changing the orbital positions leaves geometry independent quantities such as band struc- tures E(k) unchanged, but can dramatically alter geometry dependent quantities such as optical responses σ(ω). Thus, the orbital positions can be seen as a tuning parameter which can be utilised to fit geometric quantities.

FIG. 2. GaAs tight biding optical responses for different embeddings. Legend abbreviations denote: Wannier Charge Centers (WCC), Interspace Berry Connection (IBC), Abelian QGT (ABQ), Shift Current Tensor (SCT) and Wannier interpolation (REF). (a)–(c) The only independent shift current component (xyz). (d) A symmetry-disallowed shift current component (yyx). (e) Orbital embeddings in the irreducible unit cell. (f) The only independent optical conductivity component (xx).

FIG. 3. Optical conductivity ςxx for GaAs for different embeddings. Beyond the tailored fit on the Optical Conduc- tivity Tensor (OCT) and Wannier interpolation (REF), we show plots for increasing noise, corresponding to the aver- age of 15 responses computed from orbital embeddings drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation σ, and the geometry independent contribution (KPC) obtained by placing all orbitals at the origin (i.e. σ = 0).
